content: supercarto gives an AI agent a map of any location on Earth as a token-budgeted topological graph: streets as edges, crossings as junctions, indoor floors and levels as separate layers, with weather, terrain, daylight and transit riding along. Everything the agent reads is measured in tokens, so one call fits a budget — and the budget is re-measured on the emitted output, not estimated on the input. Quick start Install supercarto and return your first maplet in minutes. The tools The eleven tools a supercarto deployment advertises, and when each one exists. Honesty rules How refusal, absence, and degradation are stated — never a plausible-sounding guess. Release notes Every release, sourced from GitHub Releases. A give and a take One file in, both numbers out: examples/synthetic-dense.geojson is 272,993 bytes (~68,000 tokens) raw and compiles at a 1024-token budget to about 890 tokens — 26 nodes (10 named) on 34 edges, ~99% smaller. What the agent reads: It is standard YAML in flow style, using only constructs a model has read billions of times. The wire format is standard YAML, optimized for machines; the compiler, not the model, does the translation from raw geodata. Install The quick start has the two-minute version for Node, Python, Claude Desktop, and the hosted endpoint. Where to read next The budget is a real budget — how output is ranked, cut, kept connected, and re-measured. Honesty rules — the refusal and degradation semantics that run through every tool. Accuracy — verified distances across latitudes. Transit schedules — stops, lines, departure boards, live delays, and a certified ride plan. FAQ — the questions every evaluation starts with. Interfaces — MCP, CLI, HTTP, Python client.
description: supercarto gives an AI agent a map of any location on Earth as a token-budgeted topological graph — one call, N tokens, measured on output.
title: Introduction

content: Bug fixes: Live Overpass fetch now works for negative latitudes: supercarto emits the positional (s,w,n,e) bbox form instead of the bbox:-prefixed form, which the public Overpass instance rejects with HTTP 400 for negative-latitude boxes. Includes a regression test. Connectivity fixes for token-budgeted map graphs (PR #1, fix-connected-budget). No new features. Full details in CHANGELOG.md.

New get_transit tool over any static GTFS feed (dir or .zip via SUPERCARTO_GTFS): stops, lines, and first/last departures for the queried day, with three honest service states (running / none / unknown), past-midnight times kept as recorded (25:10), straight-line distances labelled, and a hard re-measured token budget with connection-preserving pruning. Fixed: slope heat layers no longer vanish when every surviving hotspot ties (uniformly steep terrain is a fact, not an absence) — compiler change mirrored in the Python port and parity-checked. 412 tests passing; verified against the GTFS sample feed in all three service states. Apache-2.0.
title: 0.5.0 — GTFS transit schedules for agents

content: Patch release: three honest-output fixes on the token-budget contract - the shrink loop now admits cut vertices at the small-graph exhaustion branch (a 512-budget maplet used to return 580 tokens), stale obstacle references are pruned on both ports, uniform-plateau heat collapses to its summary, and degenerate-range rel reads at the ceiling. The Python port mirrors the TS fixes exactly; pytest parity is byte-clean across fixture budgets 128-2048. Plus hosted-worker readiness fixes. 416 TS tests.
title: 0.5.1 — the budget kept its promise

content: The tile-y conversion mirrored every remote PMTiles fetch about the equator; SF streets read back at -37.77. Both ports fixed; the fixture test now asserts the hemisphere with parsed coordinates, not a digit regex that a mirror satisfies. Verified live against build.protomaps.com (lat 37.7164..37.7903 for the SF bbox). Parity gate now covers budgets 128-2048 and rebuilds a stale dist first.
title: 0.5.2 — PMTiles reads real archives at the true latitude

content: /terrain answered an honest 503 at the hosted endpoint because every real-world Terrarium tile is PNG-encoded and the bundled zero-dependency decoder read a raw-sample variant only - realistic endpoints fetched fine and decoded to nothing. Worse, once PNG decoding existed, the shared formula was wrong by a factor of 256: the two live checks that proved it were Denver reading 6.2 m (should be ~1600 m) and the Everest region reading 34 m. src/source/png.ts + port: chunk parser, scanline filters (None, Sub, Up, Average, Paeth) and the Terrarium formula R*256 + G + B/256 - 32768 metres, for 8-bit RGB/RGBA, non-interlaced. Palettes, 16-bit depth and interlace are hard rejects, not guesses. Inflate is the Web DecompressionStream in Workers and Node's zlib under Node, via zlibsafe.ts - still zero runtime npm dependencies. The raw-sample decoder now also decodes to metres ((s - 32768) / 256), and the bilinear sampler is pure interpolation over metre-valued grids. Hosted /terrain returns real elevation: SF −25..143 m, Denver 1568..1646 m, Everest region 5023..6948 m, verified live. The honest-503 reason stays for tiles that genuinely fail to decode.
title: 0.5.3 — real elevation: /terrain decodes PNG Terrarium tiles

content: Riders ask "is my bus late"; static schedules cannot answer. 0.5.4 adds the realtime half with zero runtime dependencies: Wire reader (src/source/proto.ts + python port): minimal protobuf; int32 delays arrive as 64-bit two's-complement varints; int64 times stay exact. TripUpdates schema (src/source/gtfs-rt.ts + python port): current spec field numbers (stop_time_update=2, trip-level delay=5 — both differ from the 2015-era numbers still in old tutorials), verified against the canonical proto and three live keyless agency feeds (Adelaide Metro, Sofia, Translink SEQ) — both ports decode each feed to identical counts. Deleted entities are retracted, unknown fields skip by wire type, gzipped feeds inflate. Live join in get_transit: node lines gain live: entries (bus 16 +300s, bus 16 cancelled) beside first/last; the note carries feed freshness and the load-bearing honesty line — a stop without a live entry is unknown, not on time. Absolute-time predictions convert through the feed timezone. A feed that will not read (404/timeout/malformed) degrades to the pure schedule answer with its reason quoted — never fabricated delays, never a silent drop. Config: SUPERCARTO_GTFS_RT alongside SUPERCARTO_GTFS. Also fixes a latent eval-order bug in the MVT wire readers (both languages) the live-feed trace exposed. 443 tests passing (310 unit / 121 live / 12 MCP end-to-end); parity gate green.
title: 0.5.4 — GTFS-Realtime: live delays join onto the schedule

content: next: on every transit node. Upcoming departures at that stop, in feed time order and the feed's own clock ("tram 9 25:10" stays past midnight), capped at three with the hidden rest counted (+2 more). Rows before the local query time are gone; when the day's last departure has run, the note says the day is over instead of letting an empty board read as a broken feed. Realtime joins onto the board. With SUPERCARTO_GTFS_RT set, predictions decorate their rows inline — bus 16 07:05 +300s or cancelled — using the same spec precedence as 0.5.4's live list. Predictions the board has spoken are removed from live:, so one fact renders once. Scheduling honesty. A trip-level prediction decorates only its own trip's rows; another trip's departure stays unsuffixed. A stop with no prediction is unknown, not on time. 314 unit tests (was 310), 121 live, 12 MCP e2e; parity gate green.
title: 0.5.5 — The next-departure board

content: Fix: get_transit (MCP, HTTP, CLI) fetched the realtime overlay but never joined it — a deployment with SUPERCARTO_GTFS_RT set answered schedule-only, silently. Now every public entry point joins predictions, as 0.5.4 intended and its tests (which bypassed the public path) believed had shipped. The TransitSource interface now carries the overlay parameter, so this bug class fails type check next time. Two regression tests pin the wire itself. 316 unit / 121 live / 12 MCP e2e; parity green.
title: 0.5.6 — drive the realtime join from every entry point

content: New tool get_transit_route (and CLI transit-route): walk to a stop, ride one shared line, walk it off. Straight-line walk legs, labelled as such. Never a two-line interchange — a feed cannot prove one, so the renderer refuses to invent it. Certified, not presented. Plans are certified against the service day. On an uncertified day (no calendar, no service) the note says so and plans: 0. When nothing can be certified the note names which leg failed: no stop in a catchment, no shared line, or the day's departures already run. Realtime with the board's precedence. Predicted delays decorate their trips (depart 07:00 -60s); cancelled trips drop out with a counted note; one trip's prediction is never the network's. Dense catchments search the eight nearest stops per end and say so. 458 tests: 325 unit / 121 live / 12 MCP e2e; parity gate green; Python carries the mirrored toolcatalog line only.
title: 0.5.7 — The certified ride plan

content: New: /transit-route on the HTTP server — the certified one-line ride plan over plain HTTP, same words as the MCP tool, ?format=yaml for direct reads. Override queries stop silently dropping realtime. A ?feed= query constructed its GTFS source without SUPERCARTO_GTFS_RT and never passed an overlay — 0.5.6's bug in a new coat. The server now carries the realtime URL (new gtfsRtUrl option, defaulting to the environment) and drives the fresh overlay onto the renderer in the same breath. Note sentence repair: a feed with no realtime URL configured reads "All times are scheduled; no real-time feed is configured." instead of the contradictory "Real-time feed unavailable (no real-time feed configured)". A not-configured feed is a deployment fact; a down feed is a network fact. One sentence each. HTTP tests pin the wire by riding a realtime URL that refuses connections: an override answer saying "Real-time feed unavailable" proves the attempt was driven. 461 tests: 328 unit / 121 live / 12 MCP e2e; parity gate green.
title: 0.5.8 — HTTP parity for the transit surfaces

Wire semantics unchanged — the TypeScript suite (461) and the parity gate pass. Verified live on Translink SEQ (35 MB zip): the departure-board query that previously OOMed on Node's default heap now answers on a 512 MB heap, byte-identical, and the realtime join holds at scale (757 trip predictions joined, feed 32 s old, live delay lines on the boards).
title: 0.6.1 — whole-metro feeds inside the default heap

content: Navigate to the release assets and grab supercarto-0.6.2.mcpb (384 KB). Open it with Claude Desktop and the maps tools install: the server runs from the bundle as a plain Node process with zero npm dependencies, so the only requirement on the machine is Node >= 18. Alongside the always-on tools get_maplet, localize, route, search_places, expand_feature, get_terrain, get_weather, get_daylight, the install-time configuration can wire get_traffic (needs a routing-provider key) and get_transit / get_transit_route (needs a local GTFS feed path, plus the operator's GTFS-Realtime TripUpdates URL for live per-trip delay lines). Optional install config: an Open-Meteo API key for higher weather rate limits a GTFS feed path (directory of .txt tables or a .zip) the feed operator's TripUpdates URL The manifest marks the tool catalog as generated, mirroring the server's own honest-refusal design: whatever answers introspection is exactly what that installation can answer. Verified with the official mcpb validate CLI and an unpacked-bundle initialize probe.
title: 0.6.2 — one-click install in Claude Desktop (MCPB bundle)

content: Distances are verified against haversine ground truth at mid and high latitude: 0.11% error at San Francisco (37.77°N) 0.11% error at Oslo (59.91°N) Why this required work Web Mercator distances exceed ground distance by 1/cos(latitude) on both axes. Two failure modes live in that sentence: Getting the sign wrong produces a 26% distance error at mid latitude that compounds toward the poles. A mean isotropic scale is wrong for a non-square bbox. The scale is applied per axis, so a wide bbox at 60°N does not inherit a scale chosen for its height. The benchmark spans 64°N to 33°S deliberately A benchmark run only at 37°N measures one case and hides every sign error toward the poles. Crossing hemispheres (11°S, 41°S, 33°S) in the task set is what makes "the Mercator correction is right" a checked claim rather than a symptom of luck.
description: Distances verified against haversine ground truth at mid and high latitude — the Mercator scale correction done per axis.
title: Accuracy

content: Most map-for-agents code truncates and hopes. supercarto treats truncation as a correctness problem, with four mechanisms: Ranking Named landmarks survive; anonymous intersections are cut first. An intersection named "2nd & Mission" ranks higher than an unnamed junction 100 m away, because an agent can act on a name. Connectivity Cut vertices are never removed, so the surviving network stays connected. A map the agent can traverse but not connect is worse than a smaller map it can use — "how do I get from here to there" has no answer on a severed graph. No stranded names A landmark the agent can see but cannot route to is removed. It would confidently try to walk to it — the same hallucinated-route failure mode in miniature, introduced by the cutting step itself. Verification emitAndVerify re-measures the actual emitted YAML and cuts again until it fits. The reported budget is the budget delivered, not an estimate on an intermediate representation. This is what makes the number a budget rather than a target. Why you can trust the geometry the budget delivers: the accuracy page shows distance verification across latitudes. Honesty Every drop is recorded in omitted:, aggregated per layer, so the model can tell "not there" from "not shown". An agent combining supercarto's output with other sources, or reasoning about a pharmacy that does not appear, can reason about the difference: Try it yourself supercarto bench <file.geojson> reports the token cost of any file at a budget, and the benchmark repository (supercarto-bench) holds the task-level evidence: the compiled graph scores 38/47 against 15/44 for raw GeoJSON and 0/47 for no map, re-derivable from committed archives without model calls.
description: How output gets ranked, cut, kept connected, and re-measured until the reported number is the delivered number.
title: The budget is a real budget

content: Every tool in supercarto is built on one rule, applied everywhere: a missing answer must not read like a present-and-fine answer. An agent's failure mode is not saying "I don't know"; it is saying something plausible-sounding that the person then acts on. These are the semantics that policy enforces: Situation What the deployment does What it never does No traffic credential tool not advertised; routing labels free-flow report free-flow as live congestion No GTFS feed transit tools not advertised answer "no service" Date with no scheduled service keeps stops, routes: [], says so in the note read as "the feed is broken" Feed without a calendar whole network, window declared unknown present whole-feed data as today's schedule Stop with no realtime prediction no live: entry, note says "unknown" render as "on time" Weather source unreachable degraded set, tool raises return zeroes Place with no recorded hours no hours: field at all render as closed — or open Source used is a fallback source: names the fallback, warnings travel name the primary source Public demo router route demoted to feasibility hand over fiction as fact Three states, never two The pattern underlying most rows: absence is a third state. Known-open and known-closed are facts; never-recorded is unknown. hours absent is not closed. A stop without a prediction is not on time. A no-service day is not no stops. Each distinction changes what a person should do next, so each is encoded in the output — inside the map where a model reading only one block still sees it, not on this documentation page. A developer's sketch Before a feature ships, its failure behavior is designed — at length and in the open. The honest-refusal states are part of the specification: one tool that could return "on time" for a scheduled-and-silent bus has more to prove than ten that came up short on tokens. Where this gets verified 121 of the 461 tests run against live sources; 42 cover the transit layer's service states; 5 cover the realtime join; the parity engine runs on every push and fails the release if TypeScript and Python ever disagree about a byte of output.
description: The refusal, absence, and degradation semantics that run through every tool — silence is never punctuality.
title: Honesty rules

content: Why not just paste GeoJSON into the prompt? Raw GeoJSON costs thousands of tokens per blocks-sized extract, and models reason badly and hallucinate over raw coordinates. In head-to-head task benchmarks, a compiled supercarto graph scores 38/47 while raw GeoJSON for the same places scores 15/44 and no map scores 0/47. Does supercarto need an API key for map data? No. Live OpenStreetMap data over Overpass needs no key, and Open-Meteo weather and Terrarium elevation need no key either. For production volume you can point supercarto at your own PMTiles archive. Live traffic is the only feature that needs a key (TomTom or HERE). How does it not overflow the context window? You set a token budget. The compiler ranks features, keeps named landmarks, removes anonymous intersections first, and guarantees the surviving network stays connected. Every removal is recorded in the omitted: section, so the model can tell "not there" from "not shown". Is there a hosted version? Yes, a honest subset: a compilation endpoint answers /maplet and /scr over HTTP, weather and rate limiting are live, and terrain, transit and traffic are stated as absent with reasons. Transit needs a local feed; hosted mode ships no flow keys. What license, what tests? Apache-2.0. 461 tests: unit (including transit states, protobuf wire, realtime join, PNG elevation decoder), 121 against live sources, and 12 MCP end-to-end. Outputs are byte-identical to the Python port; the parity gate runs on every push. What is deliberately not implemented? Hosted vector tiles with style delivery, and full indoor room geometry beyond centroids. Both are stated here rather than shipped half-way.
description: Short answers to the questions every evaluation starts with.
title: FAQ

content: Everything is read from the environment by one factory, so the CLI and the MCP server cannot disagree about where data came from — they did once, and nothing reported it. Source Status Configure Overpass default OVERPASS_ENDPOINT (your own instance for volume) PMTiles / Protomaps opt-in, then primary SUPERCARTO_PMTILES=https://your-bucket/planet.pmtiles OSRM opt-in for turn-by-turn point the env at an engine you host and have verified Open-Meteo default key optional: SUPERCARTO_OWM_KEY TomTom / HERE key required TOMTOM_API_KEY / HERE_API_KEY Terrarium tiles default TERRARIUM_ENDPOINT GTFS feed opt-in SUPERCARTO_GTFS (dir or zip) GTFS-Realtime with a feed SUPERCARTO_GTFS_RT (TripUpdates URL) Toggle switches: SUPERCARTO_PMTILES — PMTiles archive URL; primary source when set OVERPASS_ENDPOINT — your own Overpass instance TERRARIUM_ENDPOINT — elevation tile template TOMTOM_API_KEY / HERE_API_KEY — enables get_traffic SUPERCARTO_GTFS — path to a GTFS feed (dir or .zip); enables the transit tools SUPERCARTO_GTFS_RT — TripUpdates URL; adds live delay lines PMTiles is the answer at production volume Range requests against object storage, milliseconds, no rate limit — and the reader is included: no pmtiles dependency, no mapbox-gl, zero transitive packages. A built-in MVT decoder walks the archive in-process. Whole-metro feeds, default heap Since 0.6.1 the GTFS load is columnar — stop_times parse straight into per-trip arrays, no row objects — so a feed the size of Translink SEQ (35 MB zip) fits Node's default heap and the answer is byte-identical to the pre-0.6.1 build. Verified live: schedule, departure boards, and 750+ realtime predictions join in one answer, no NODE_OPTIONS needed. GTFS at scale, and the honesty of absence A feed is only as fresh as the operator's last import, and a schedule that exists but is stale is worse than absent: the tool must not be advertised at all unless the operator has wired one. With realtime configured, a stop without a prediction reads as unknown — never on time — and the note says so in words:
description: Where every layer gets its data — env-controlled, one factory, honest fallbacks.
title: Data sources

content: Local HTTP Full surface: maplets, SCR, transit, transit-route, health. Cloudflare Worker The compile path is Workers-compatible (fetch-based sources, no Node built-ins), and cloud/worker/ packages it as a Cloudflare Worker: the same /maplet, /scr, weather, daylight and terrain surface as the local HTTP API, with per-IP rate limiting and ODbL attribution on every map response. cloud/worker/ src wrangler.jsonc README.md It is deliberately a subset, stated on GET /: transit and traffic are not served — a Worker has no filesystem for a GTFS feed, and hosted mode ships no flow-provider keys the archive fallback (protomaps source line) is coarse beyond z10-ish, and tile/feature fetches are capped so a request stays inside a Worker CPU budget terrain answers 503 rather than a rough answer: Terrarium tiles are PNG-encoded and the bundled zero-dependency decoder reads raw buffers only GET /healthz probes Overpass only, so a 503 there means the Overpass leg is unreachable — not that the PMTiles fallback is down Every hosted answer says what it cannot serve. An excerpt cannot mislead a model about what a full deployment would answer. What the source line carries The source: field names what actually served the data (overpass or protomaps), because the shared Overpass instances refuse the shared Cloudflare egress range for this deployment — the fallback is what actually answers, and the document says so.
description: Local HTTP, the hosted Cloudflare Worker and its honest subsets, plus documentation site deployment.
title: Deployment

content: The CLI runs the same library as the MCP server. One binary, every surface: Command What it does supercarto fetch --lat --lon --radiusM --budget compile a maplet; --layers filters; --metrics reports tokens supercarto weather --lat --lon --hours forecast supercarto traffic --from --to traffic or the labelled free-flow answer supercarto transit --feed --lat --lon --radiusM departure boards from a GTFS feed supercarto route --from --to --mode feasibility answer supercarto compile <file.geojson> --budget compile a local GeoJSON into a maplet supercarto encode <file.geojson> --out SCR codec to a compact file supercarto decode <file.scr> back from SCR supercarto bench <file.geojson> token-cost check supercarto mcp MCP server over stdio supercarto serve --port HTTP API maplet transit traffic weather Failure behavior fetch layers accept road and poi alongside raw OSM tags; anything else is rejected rather than silently returning nothing. A request that would yield named places with no streets fails with a clear error — pass --layers poi for a POI-only map. Warnings travel inside the map output, not just stderr, so an agent that reads only the map sees them.
description: Every supercarto command, from fetch to decode, with the flags each one takes.
title: CLI

content: Boot the API locally: It serves GET /maplet, GET /scr, GET /transit and GET /transit-route, each answering YAML (format=yaml) or JSON. GET /health reports the server's cache health. GET /maplet lat · query · number · required Latitude in [-90, 90]. lon · query · number · required Longitude in [-180, 180]. radiusM · query · integer · default 300 Radius in metres, clamped to the machine's limit. budget · query · integer · default 1024 Token budget for the emitted YAML. layers · query · string Comma-separated layer filter. format · query · string · default json yaml returns the agent-ready document directly. Errors are honest too A deployment with no GTFS feed configured answers 404 with "no GTFS feed configured for this deployment" rather than a transcript-shaped "no service" — the refusal names the action (set SUPERCARTO_GTFS or pass ?feed=) that makes the tool exist. GET /transit Same parameter style: lat, lon, radiusM, budget, at (the instant to evaluate), and format. The per-deployment feed comes from SUPERCARTO_GTFS; a specific request can name its own feed with ?feed=<dir or zip>, and the operator's SUPERCARTO_GTFS_RT follows feed overrides, so a feed override never silently drops live data. GET /transit-route Adds fromLat, fromLon, toLat, toLon, and maxWalkM. The answer is the certified ride plan.
description: The maplet, screen, transit and route endpoints, with parameters and examples.
title: HTTP API

content: supercarto is an MCP server. Point an MCP client at it: The tool list is per-deployment: eight tools with nothing configured, and get_traffic / get_transit / get_transit_route appear exactly when their operator configuration exists. Introspection never lists a tool whose answer would be a guess. Claude Desktop in one click Tell your browsing agent to install supercarto Add https://github.com/Unselfisheologism/supercarto as an MCP server on glama.ai under my logged-in account. If asked how it runs: stdio, command npx supercarto mcp, no API key needed. Or skip agents entirely: every release publishes an MCPB bundle — download supercarto-X.Y.Z.mcpb from the latest release and open it with Claude Desktop. Install-time configuration can wire the weather key, a local GTFS feed path, and the operator's TripUpdates URL. The server has zero npm dependencies, so the bundle itself is 384 KB. Tool honesty on the wire The three conditional tools exist or don't. There is no stub, no empty array, no "feed not configured" pretence dressed as an answer: a manifest tools_generated: true plus per-maplet tools: blocks keep every introspection surface in sync with what can actually run. One factory Environment configuration is read by one factory (see data sources), so the CLI and the MCP server cannot disagree about where data came from — they did once, and nothing reported it.
description: supercarto exposes MCP over stdio; one-click install ships as an MCPB bundle.
title: MCP and Claude Desktop

content: The Python package is a client, not a port of the compiler. It speaks JSON-RPC to the Node server over stdio, because the mcp package would pull in httpx and pydantic, and an agent framework that already depends on one of them should not get a second copy. Async Notes maplet (accepts radius_m snake_case) compiles a topological graph, exactly the YAML the Node API returns — the byte-parity gate verifies the port agrees. weather returns the same structured answer, degraded the same way (raises when the source is down, never zeroes). The client requires the Node server (npx supercarto mcp or a global install) on PATH. Zero runtime dependencies This holds by design on both sides: the Node server installs nothing, the Python client imports nothing. The byte-parity gate fails the build if either side starts depending on something, or if a byte of output ever disagrees.
description: An asyncio client with zero runtime dependencies, speaking JSON-RPC to the Node server over stdio.
title: Python client

content: supercarto needs Node.js 20+ (server) and nothing else: zero runtime npm dependencies, no database, no API key. A coordinate and a token budget are the whole interface. npm pip The Python client speaks JSON-RPC to the Node server over stdio rather than importing an SDK, so it carries zero runtime dependencies of its own. npx (no install) Claude Desktop Download the latest release bundle and open the supercarto-X.Y.Z.mcpb file with Claude Desktop — one click, and the tools install with optional configuration (weather key, GTFS feed path). The bundle is 384 KB. Your first maplet result.yaml is a standard-YAML topological graph: named nodes, edges with distances in metres and compass directions, an omitted: record of everything cut, and the tools the agent can call next. The same answer, from the CLI: Turn it into an MCP server The one process answers MCP over stdio: Standard mcpServers configuration for any MCP client: Like it as a bundle instead? Three more appear only when their configuration exists — see the tools. Deployment surfaces CLI fetch, weather, traffic, transit, route, compile, encode, decode, bench, mcp, serve. title: Quick start

content: A supercarto deployment advertises exactly what it can answer. Eight tools exist with no configuration at all; three appear only when the operator's environment backs them. Nothing ever advertises a tool whose answer would read like a guess. Tool Needs Answers get_maplet nothing what is near this coordinate localize nothing what changed after the agent or the person moved route nothing straight-line distance, direction, walking feasibility search_places nothing find places by name or type expand_feature nothing exact geometry for one feature get_terrain nothing ground elevation and slope get_weather nothing current conditions and forecast get_daylight nothing sun position, sunrise, sunset get_traffic TomTom or HERE key congestion and realistic arrival time get_transit GTFS feed stops, lines, service times, departure boards get_transit_route GTFS feed certified one-line ride plan The rule behind the table: a tool with no flow provider behind it reports one honest free-flow number and labels it; a schedule tool with no schedule behind it would teach a model to trust "no feed" as an answer that reads like "no service" — so it is not a tool at all until an operator imports a feed. get_maplet The whole product: a walkable graph in one call. localize Move the session for the cost of the delta. route Feasibility, not turn-by-turn. search_places / expand_feature Query on the map, then expand geometry one feature at a time. get_terrain / get_daylight Ground truth and sun position; no key, no archive. get_weather Keyless forecast with a degraded path that refuses to invent readings. get_traffic Live with a key; labelled free-flow without one. get_transit / get_transit_route Schedules, boards, live delays, and the certified ride plan.
description: The eleven tools a supercarto deployment advertises, and exactly when each one exists.
title: The tools

content: always advertised get_maplet(lat, lon, radius, layers, budget) — the single call that produces the product. Fetches real geodata around a coordinate, compiles a topological graph, cuts it to your budget, and emits YAML. Prop Type Default Description lat number - Latitude in [-90, 90]. lon number - Longitude in [-180, 180]. radius? number - Radius in metres. Kept sane at the interface. budget? number - Token budget for the emitted YAML. layers? string[] - Layer filter. Raw OSM tag selectors are also taken; anything else is rejected rather than silently returning nothing. The output Nodes, edges, and — this is the part that makes it honest — omissions: Order of operations Ranking first (named landmarks survive), then connectivity-preserving cuts (a cut vertex is never removed), then stranded-name removal (a landmark the agent cannot route to is removed), then re-measure the actual emitted YAML and cut again until it fits. The budget is the budget delivered, not an estimate. What a node can carry Beyond topology: hours (evaluated in the map's timezone — a known-closed shop at 04:00 reads closed, a bench with no recorded hours emits no hours at all), sun and twilight in the map header, transit nodes, indoor floors, and the tools: list at the foot. The omitted: section exists so the model can tell not there from not shown. An agent reading only this block still knows the map is an excerpt.
description: The core call — a walkable, token-budgeted topological graph of any coordinate.
title: get_maplet

content: always advertised get_terrain get_terrain(lat, lon, radiusM, samples) — ground elevation and slope around a coordinate, from Terrarium-encoded tiles. No key; the default endpoint is the AWS Open Data elevation archive, overridable with TERRARIUM_ENDPOINT. Slope is what changes "a park 400 m away" into "a park 400 m away and 60 m up a hill the wheelchair cannot climb". get_daylight get_daylight(lat, lon, at) — sun position, sunrise, sunset, twilight band, and whether a light is needed. Always available: sun position is arithmetic, needing no source and no credential, so this tool never disappears from a deployment. The twilight band is not a boolean. Walking is fine at civil twilight and unwise at nautical, so the band names one of day, civil, nautical, night. Above the Arctic circles the map reports polar: day or polar: night instead of inventing a sunrise.
description: Ground elevation and slope, sun position, sunrise and sunset — arithmetic and tiles, no keys.
title: get_terrain and get_daylight

content: advertised only with a key get_traffic(from, to, mode) — congestion level and a realistic arrival time for a drive, from the worst segment rather than an average. Exists, or doesn't Traffic needs a credential, so get_traffic is absent from the tool list until TOMTOM_API_KEY or HERE_API_KEY is set. With no key the routing path still reports speed, but labels it: The single most damaging thing this library could do A free-flow estimate for a congested route is worse than no answer, because the person leaves on the schedule the agent gave them. Presenting one as live is precisely what the honest-refusal design exists to prevent — hence the label travels with the number, and the tool itself does not exist until a provider does.
description: Live congestion with a provider key; labelled free-flow without one.
title: get_traffic

content: advertised only with a GTFS feed Set SUPERCARTO_GTFS to any static GTFS feed — a directory of .txt tables or a .zip — and two tools appear. Add SUPERCARTO_GTFS_RT (the operator's TripUpdates URL) and their answers gain live per-trip information. get_transit get_transit(lat, lon, radiusM, budget) — transit stops, lines, and a service window for the queried day, from the GTFS feed: Three service states, never two A running day shows today's routes and departures. A date with nothing running keeps the stops with routes: [] and a note saying no service runs — no transit is not no stops. A feed with no calendar shows the whole network and declares the service window unknown, rather than labelling whole-feed facts as today's schedule. Times past midnight stay past midnight GTFS writes a departure after the service day's midnight as 25:10. Re-rendering it as 01:10 fits the eye and strands the person waiting. It renders as recorded, in the feed's own timezone, with the evaluated instant in the note. Edges are structure; schedules attach to nodes The adjacency survives a no-service day, because an agent walking between stops still wants to know the stops are 601 m apart. Departure boards, not just the day's window A next: attribute lists upcoming departures at each stop, in feed time and the feed's clock, capped at three with the hidden rest counted (+7 more). With realtime configured the board speaks the prediction inline: bus 16 07:05 +300s or cancelled. Live delays, and what absence means GTFS-Realtime TripUpdates join onto the schedule: live: attributes like bus 16 +300s or bus 16 cancelled, feed-freshness stated in the note. A stop with no prediction has no live entry — unknown, not on time — and the note says so in words. Whole-metro scale in the default heap Since 0.6.1 the feed load is columnar: a Translink SEQ–size feed (35 MB zip) loads inside Node's default heap with byte-identical output, and boards join 750+ trip predictions in one answer. get_transit_route get_transit_route(fromLat, fromLon, toLat, toLon, maxWalkM, budget) — a certified ride plan between two coordinates: walk to a stop, ride one line that serves both catchments, walk it off. The rule that makes it trustworthy: never an interchange a feed cannot prove. If no single line connects both ends within the walk limits, the note names the leg that failed — it does not invent a two-line itinerary that "probably works". Plans ride on the departure board's honesty: certified against the service day, predictions decorate their trips, cancelled trips drop out with a counted note, and all walking legs are labelled straight-line.
description: Schedules, departure boards, live delays, and a certified ride plan — honest in all three service states.
title: get_transit and get_transit_route

content: always advertised get_weather(lat, lon, hours) — current conditions and an hourly forecast from Open-Meteo. No key, no account, no billing; an optional SUPERCARTO_OWM_KEY lifts the rate limit. Prose, not fields The MCP tool returns prose rather than number-fields, because a model repeats "it is raining, take the bus" reliably, and re-derives it from twelve numbers unreliably. The degraded path When the source is unreachable the library sets degraded and the tool raises. It does not return zeroes. Why zeros are the failure An agent handed precipitationMm: 0 concludes the weather is dry and sends someone cycling into a storm. Absence of a weather reading is not the same thing as absence of rain — a missing answer must announce itself as missing.
description: Keyless current conditions and forecast, with a degraded path that refuses to invent readings.
title: get_weather

content: always advertised localize(scr, lat, lon, radius, layers, budget) — you already hold a maplet and the person moved. A new get_maplet call would re-pay for every unchanged node; localize returns only what changed: nodes appeared, disappeared, or shifted, edges re-wired, and the same honesty records. When the prompt is already long and the user says "the other corner", this is the cheap path — a district stays affordable, a street corner cheaper. Cheap compared to what A maplet's token cost is dominated by nodes and edges the previous maplet already contained. localize exists so a moving session never pays that cost twice.
description: Move an open map session for the cost of the delta, not a new map.
title: localize

content: always advertised route(from, to, mode) — straight-line distance, compass direction, and whether the approach is walkable, from one coordinate to another. Why not turn-by-turn by default Routing APIs sometimes return confident nonsense — in benchmark work the public demo OSRM answered Ok with a walk route that covered a straight-line half-kilometre in 40 seconds. A tool whose default path can invent a route through water is worse than a tool that refuses. So route is a feasibility answer: distance, direction, then "verify the approach on arrival". Turn-by-turn exists only with OSRM, opt-in, for an engine you host and have verified (see data sources). Do not hand supercarto's demo defaults to a production agent The route tool with no OSRM configured states its limits in its answer. Fine for "roughly how far is the café". If the trip's success depends on the route, self-host a routing engine and point the env at it.
description: Feasibility first — straight-line distance, direction, and walking verification.
title: route

content: always advertised search_places search_places(lat, lon, radius, query, limit) — find places by name or type within the maplet's catchment. This is the "where do I meet them" query: give it names of things ("pharmacy", "Blue Bottle") and ranked matches come back as node ids. expand_feature expand_feature(id) — exact geometry for one feature in this maplet. The budget cut keeps landmarks but simplifies their geometry; when an agent actually needs the full shape of one building, park, or floor, it expands just that feature instead of re-paying for the whole area. The two tools work as a pair: budget keeps context cheap, expansion keeps detail reachable. The tools: block at the foot of every maplet advertises which of these its own catchment can answer.
description: Query a maplet by name or type, then expand one feature's exact geometry on demand.
title: search_places and expand_feature
